subject: Cooking
title: The Chemistry of Tea Oxidation
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Chemistry of Tea Oxidation usable.

hook.text: Green tea and black tea start as the same leaf. The difference? Controlled damage that triggers oxidation.

buildup.text: When tea leaves are bruised or rolled, enzymes called polyphenol oxidases react with oxygen in the air.

discovery.text: Green tea is heated immediately to stop oxidation. Oolong is partially oxidized. Black tea is fully oxidized.

twist.text: The process isn't fermentation — despite being called that for centuries. True fermentation occurs only in pu-erh tea.

climax.text: Oxidation converts catechins (green tea's antioxidants) into theaflavins (black tea's bold flavor compounds).

punchline.text: Same leaf. Different damage. Completely different drink.

quiz.question: What process turns green tea leaves into black tea?

details.summary: Tea type is determined by oxidation — the enzymatic browning that occurs when tea leaves are damaged and polyphenols react with oxygen. Green tea is minimally oxidized by quick heating. Oolong is partially oxidized. Black tea is fully oxidized.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding oxidation reveals that all tea comes from one plant and processing determines everything. This knowledge transforms tea selection from guesswork into informed choice.
takeaways: All tea types come from the same Camellia sinensis plant
Oxidation level determines color, flavor, and antioxidant content
Green tea stops oxidation early; black tea allows full oxidation

faq.question: How does oxidation change tea flavor?
faq.answer: Fresh unoxidized leaves are vegetal and astringent from catechins. As oxidation progresses, catechins convert to theaflavins and thearubigins, which are less bitter and produce malty, fruity, sweet notes. Full oxidation in black tea yields robust, smooth flavors.

faq.question: Does green tea have more antioxidants than black tea?
faq.answer: Green tea retains more catechins because minimal oxidation preserves these compounds. However, black tea's theaflavins and thearubigins are also powerful antioxidants — just different ones.
